stem: A law firm replaces its own on-premises mail servers with a software as a service (SaaS) email offering. Under the shared responsibility model, which security task is still the firm's responsibility after the move?

choices.text: Securing the physical hosts, network hardware and datacenter buildings where the mailboxes are stored.
Deciding who in the firm can use the service and how the firm's tenant-level security settings are configured.
Maintaining the runtime environment and the application code that deliver mail to the firm's mailboxes.
Applying security updates to the operating systems of the servers that run the email service for the firm.

stem: A team moves a line-of-business application from its datacenter onto virtual machines that it creates in a public cloud (infrastructure as a service). Which security duty does the team keep that a platform as a service offering would have taken over?

choices.text: Classifying the application's data and deciding which users are allowed to read the stored records.
Replacing failed disks and network cards in the physical host machines that run the virtual machines.
Patching and hardening the operating system installed on each virtual machine that the team created.
Physical security of the datacenter, including badge readers and guards at the doors of the building.

stem: Employees use an AI assistant delivered as a SaaS service. The assistant is connected to internal documents, and the security team worries that hidden instructions inside those documents could manipulate its answers. Under the AI shared responsibility model, who must address this risk?

choices.text: Nobody in particular, because prompt injection affects only AI models that the customer trains on its own hardware.
The provider alone, because it hosts the AI model and runs the platform-level content filtering for every tenant.
The provider alone, because connecting a SaaS assistant to internal documents makes those documents provider data.
The customer, through access controls, the connectors it enables, input validation and monitoring of the AI's use.

stem: In a defense-in-depth strategy, a company divides its network into isolated zones and uses network security groups to restrict which systems can talk to each other. Which layer is the company strengthening?

choices.text: The network security layer, which controls communication between resources inside the network itself.
The identity and access layer, which authenticates and authorizes users before they reach any resource.
The compute security layer, which keeps virtual machine operating systems patched and closes unused ports.
The perimeter security layer, which protects the network boundary with DDoS protection and edge firewalls.

stem: An IT manager has two needs: confirming that downloaded software files were not altered, and making sure that changes to finance records can be detected. Which TWO controls mainly protect the integrity of data? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Load balancing across redundant servers so that the finance application stays online.
Comparing the cryptographic hash of each file with the value the publisher has published.
Regular backups with tested recovery plans that restore service after a hardware failure.
Distributed denial-of-service protection that filters attack traffic before it reaches services.
Digital signatures applied by the sender with a private key and verified with its public key.

stem: A company stops giving administrators permanent admin rights. Instead, an administrator receives elevated access only for the specific task and only for the hours that task needs, and then it is removed. Which Zero Trust principle does this put into practice?

choices.text: Use least privileged access, because access is limited with just-in-time and just-enough-access practices.
Assume breach, because the network is segmented and all traffic is encrypted end to end between the zones.
Verify explicitly, because every request is authenticated using all available signals such as device and location.
Trust the internal network, because administrators work from the corporate office on managed company devices.

stem: A security architect designs the environment as if attackers are already inside: workloads are split into segments, data is encrypted end to end, and analytics watch for unusual activity so intrusions are found fast. Which Zero Trust principle drives this design?

choices.text: Verify explicitly, which bases every access decision on identity, device health, location and other signals.
Use least privileged access, which grants only the minimum permissions a person needs for a limited time.
Defense at the perimeter, which keeps attackers out with strong firewalls at the edge of the corporate network.
Assume breach, which limits the blast radius and focuses on detecting and containing attackers quickly.

stem: In the Zero Trust model, one pillar aggregates and correlates signals from identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure and networks, and triggers automated responses using SIEM and SOAR tools. Which pillar is this?

choices.text: The applications pillar, which gives visibility into sanctioned and unsanctioned apps used across the organization.
The infrastructure pillar, which continuously assesses servers for version currency and configuration compliance.
The visibility, automation, and orchestration pillar, which integrates the signals of the other six pillars.
The networks pillar, which applies micro-segmentation, real-time threat protection and encrypted network traffic.

stem: Two companies need to exchange encrypted files over the internet, but they have no secure way to agree on a shared secret key beforehand. Which approach solves this key distribution problem?

choices.text: Asymmetric encryption, because anyone can encrypt with a freely shared public key that only the private key opens.
Hashing, because each file is converted into a fixed-length digest that only the receiving company can reverse.
Symmetric encryption, because the same secret key is used to encrypt and decrypt, so it is the fastest to share.
Salting, because a random value is added to each file so that the two companies no longer need any keys at all.

stem: An application stores user passwords as hashes. Auditors warn that an attacker who steals the database could look up common passwords in precomputed rainbow tables, and that users with the same password have identical hashes. What best addresses both findings?

choices.text: Encrypt the passwords with a symmetric key instead, so that the stored values can be decrypted later when needed.
Store the plain-text passwords in a separate database on a server that is not connected to the internet at all.
Hash every password twice with the same algorithm, so the stored value is longer and harder for attackers to guess.
Add a unique random salt to each password before hashing it, so identical passwords produce different hashes.

stem: A bank already encrypts customer data at rest in storage and in transit with TLS. It also wants the data protected while it is loaded into memory and processed on shared cloud hardware. Which approach addresses this state of data?

choices.text: Full-disk encryption on the storage accounts, which keeps data unreadable if the physical media are stolen.
HTTPS for every connection, so that the data moving between the browser and the servers cannot be read.
Confidential computing, which processes the data inside protected secure enclaves isolated from the host.
A VPN connection between offices, which protects traffic that crosses public networks between locations.

stem: A company encrypts its databases and now needs a policy for its encryption keys. Which TWO practices follow key management guidance? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Store the keys in the same storage account as the encrypted data so that applications always find them quickly.
Rotate the keys regularly so that the amount of data exposed if one key is compromised stays limited.
Give every developer and administrator read access to the keys so that troubleshooting is never blocked.
Use one permanent key for all data indefinitely so that older backups can always be decrypted without lookups.
Keep keys in tamper-resistant hardware security modules or a managed key service, separate from the data.

stem: A retailer collects customer data in France, stores it in a cloud region in Germany and analyzes it with a service running in the United States. Its lawyers say the data is subject to the laws of each of these locations. Which compliance concept are they describing?

choices.text: Data classification, which labels each record by sensitivity so that the strongest protections go to it first.
Data residency, which governs only the single physical location where the data must be stored by contract.
Data integrity, which keeps the records accurate and unmodified except through authorized business processes.
Data sovereignty, which says data is subject to the laws of each country or region where it is held or processed.

stem: During risk management, a company finds that a regional flood could damage its warehouse systems. It decides to buy an insurance policy that covers the financial losses from such an event. Which risk response is this?

choices.text: Mitigate the risk, because the company implements technical controls that reduce how likely the flood is.
Accept the risk, because the company decides the impact is low and takes no further action against it.
Transfer the risk, because another party takes on the financial impact through a measure such as insurance.
Avoid the risk, because the company changes or stops the process that creates the risk in the first place.

stem: A company launches a shopping app that collects names, email addresses and location history from its customers. Which TWO obligations come from data privacy requirements? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Proving to auditors that the company's information security management system is certified.
Being transparent about what personal data is collected and how the company uses it.
Storing every record in a data center located in the country where the company is registered.
Keeping the shopping app available to customers even during a denial-of-service attack.
Letting individuals exercise rights over their data, such as access, correction or deletion.

stem: A user signs in to a company portal with her password and an approval on her phone, and the sign-in succeeds. When she opens the payroll report, the portal shows "Access denied". Which process denied her request?

choices.text: Authorization, because the portal checked what her confirmed identity is allowed to access.
Federation, because the portal did not trust the identity provider that issued her security token.
Authentication, because the portal could not confirm that she is the person she claims to be.
Auditing, because the portal recorded the sign-in event and blocked further activity after it.

stem: A company wants to require multifactor authentication (MFA) for remote sign-ins. Which sign-in combination actually meets the definition of MFA?

choices.text: A password followed by a six-digit PIN, both typed in by the user on the sign-in page of the portal.
A username followed by a password, both checked against the company's directory at each sign-in.
A password followed by answers to two security questions that the user chose during registration.
A password followed by approving a notification on the user's registered mobile phone at sign-in.

stem: Security leaders explain why the corporate network boundary, enforced by firewalls and VPN gateways, is no longer a reliable security boundary and why identity has become the primary perimeter. Which TWO trends support this view? (Select TWO)

choices.text: All employees now work only from the main office on company-managed desktops connected by cable.
Partners and contractors are always given accounts inside the internal domain and connect over VPN.
Business-critical email and line-of-business apps now run as cloud and SaaS services outside the network.
Applications are now hosted only on servers in the company's own datacenter behind the firewall.
Employees connect from home and public Wi-Fi, so their traffic may never pass through the perimeter.

stem: After a security incident, investigators need to know which account accessed a file share, at what time and from which location. Which pillar of an identity infrastructure provides this information?

choices.text: Auditing, which tracks who did what, when and from where through sign-in logs and activity reports.
Administration, which covers creating, updating and removing identities as people join, move and leave.
Authorization, which evaluates permissions and context and then grants or restricts access to resources.
Authentication, which challenges an identity for credentials and verifies that it is who it claims to be.

stem: A company has fifteen web applications, and each one keeps its own user accounts and password rules. It wants every app to rely on one central service that verifies users and issues security tokens the apps trust. What is this central service called?

choices.text: A domain controller, which applies Group Policy settings to Windows computers joined to a domain.
An identity provider, which authenticates users and issues tokens that the applications accept as proof.
A certificate authority, which issues digital certificates that bind public keys to named organizations.
A directory service, which stores objects such as users, groups and devices for an on-premises network.

stem: After a user signs in, an identity provider issues two security tokens. The application uses one to learn the user's name and unique identifier, and uses the other to call a calendar API on the user's behalf. Which token is used to call the API?

choices.text: The session cookie, because the identity provider stores the user's permissions inside the browser cookie.
A single claim, because each claim inside a token is a separate credential that the API checks on its own.
The access token, because it grants the application permission to access a specific resource for the user.
The ID token, because it is the proof that the user signed in successfully and identifies the user.

stem: A developer builds a mobile app that must let users sign in and must then read their files from a cloud API with delegated permission. Which pairing of standard protocols matches these two jobs?

choices.text: OpenID Connect for the sign-in and OAuth 2.0 for the access tokens used to call the file API.
SAML for the mobile sign-in, because it is the protocol built for modern cloud and mobile applications.
OAuth 2.0 for the sign-in and SAML for the file API, because SAML is the protocol that issues access tokens.
Kerberos for the sign-in and NTLM for the file API, because both work natively over the public internet.

stem: An employee leaves a company that uses single sign-on (SSO) through one identity provider for all of its business applications. What is the main security benefit of SSO in this situation?

choices.text: SSO deletes the files the user created in every connected app, so no company data remains under the leaver's name.
Disabling the user's account in the identity provider removes the access to every connected application at once.
SSO turns on multifactor authentication in every app by itself, so the former employee's password alone becomes useless.
SSO gives each app its own copy of the user's password, so every app owner can lock the account independently.

stem: A company runs an on-premises Windows domain. When employees sign in to their office PCs, a server checks their credentials using Kerberos and applies Group Policy settings to the computers. What is this server?

choices.text: A web application proxy, which publishes internal websites to users who work outside the office.
A file server, which stores shared folders and applies permissions to the files that users open.
A certificate authority, which issues and revokes digital certificates for the company's servers.
A domain controller, which is a server running Active Directory Domain Services for the domain.

stem: A company that relies only on Active Directory Domain Services plans to adopt SaaS apps and support staff who work remotely on phones. Which TWO limitations of AD DS will it run into? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AD DS cannot store groups of users, so permissions must be assigned to each person's account one by one.
AD DS gives each user a separate identity for every on-premises system instead of one identity across them.
AD DS cannot apply Group Policy settings to Windows computers that are joined to the on-premises domain.
AD DS does not natively support modern protocols such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect used by cloud apps.
Users away from the corporate network cannot authenticate directly to AD DS without a VPN connection.

stem: Company A configured its identity provider to trust Company B's identity provider, so Company B's staff can open Company A's project portal with their own credentials. Company A's staff now find they cannot sign in to Company B's resources the same way. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Federation removes the need for any trust settings, so Company B's portal must be using local accounts only.
Federation always requires each user to create a separate new account in the other organization's directory.
Federation trust is not automatically bidirectional, so Company B must also configure trust for Company A.
Federation works only between two identity providers from the same vendor using the same version of software.

stem: A consumer app lets new customers sign in with their existing Google, Microsoft or GitHub accounts instead of creating a new username and password for the app. Which identity concept does this sign-in use?

choices.text: Domain join, which registers each customer's device in the app company's Active Directory domain for sign-in.
Federation, because the app trusts an external identity provider to authenticate the customer on its behalf.
Multifactor authentication, because a social account counts as a second category of authentication factor.
Directory synchronization, which copies each customer's account from the social site into the app's own database.

stem: A company keeps its on-premises Active Directory Domain Services and wants those users to reach a cloud application by authenticating against an on-premises server that issues tokens the cloud service accepts. Which Microsoft technology fits this federation scenario?

choices.text: Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS), a server role that shares identity information with external services.
NTLM authentication, which the cloud application calls directly over the internet to check each user's password.
Organizational units, which group users and computers in the directory so they are easier to administer.
Group Policy, which pushes configuration settings to every Windows computer that is joined to the on-premises domain.

stem: An online retailer runs its storefront on virtual machines in an Azure virtual network with public IP addresses. It has not purchased anything for DDoS defense. Management now wants access to Microsoft's DDoS rapid response team during attacks and service credits for scale-out costs caused by a documented attack. What should the retailer enable?

choices.text: Azure DDoS Network Protection on the virtual network, which adds DDoS rapid response support and cost protection to the core mitigation
Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway, which handles volumetric attacks and provides rapid response and cost protection
Azure Firewall Premium in front of the VMs, whose intrusion detection signatures include DDoS rapid response and cost guarantees
Nothing extra, because the default Azure DDoS infrastructure protection already includes rapid response support and cost protection

stem: A small company exposes only two public IP addresses in Azure: one for a web server VM and one for an API server VM. It wants DDoS mitigation tuned to these resources at the lowest cost, without creating a DDoS protection plan, and it does not need the rapid response team. Which option fits best?

choices.text: Network security groups with deny rules on both subnets, because they drop flood traffic before it reaches Azure
Azure DDoS IP Protection enabled on each of the two public IP resources, billed per protected IP address
Azure Firewall Basic deployed in front of both resources, because it includes DDoS mitigation for its public IPs
Azure DDoS Network Protection with a protection plan linked to the virtual network that holds both resources

stem: A company has eight Azure subscriptions in one Microsoft Entra tenant, each with virtual networks that host public-facing services. It wants Azure DDoS Network Protection for all of them. How should it plan the DDoS protection plans?

choices.text: Create one DDoS protection plan in each subscription, because a plan can only protect virtual networks in its own subscription
Create no plan, because DDoS Network Protection is switched on automatically for every subscription in the tenant
Create a single DDoS protection plan and use it for virtual networks across the subscriptions in the tenant
Create one DDoS protection plan per virtual network, because each plan learns the traffic profile of exactly one network

stem: A security lead is explaining to new staff what Azure DDoS Network Protection does once it is enabled on a virtual network. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It inspects HTTP requests for SQL injection and cross-site scripting and blocks them at the application layer
It decrypts outbound TLS traffic so that malware inside encrypted sessions can be detected and blocked
It requires each protected application to be redeployed with a DDoS agent before mitigation can start working
It learns each protected resource's traffic over time and adjusts the mitigation profile as the traffic changes
It monitors application traffic patterns around the clock and automatically mitigates an attack as soon as it is detected

stem: A company has several spoke virtual networks in Azure. It wants one managed, stateful service that controls outbound internet traffic from all of them, allowing only approved fully qualified domain names such as an update site, and logs every allowed and denied connection. Which service should it deploy?

choices.text: Network security groups on every subnet, with outbound rules that list the approved domain names for each spoke
Azure Firewall in a central virtual network, with application rules that allow only the approved domain names
Azure DDoS Network Protection on each spoke, with a protection plan that blocks traffic to unapproved domains
Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway, which filters outbound requests from virtual machines

stem: A payment processor is moving a card-processing workload to Azure. Its auditors require the network firewall to decrypt and inspect outbound TLS traffic and to run signature-based intrusion detection and prevention. Which Azure Firewall SKU meets this?

choices.text: Any Azure Firewall SKU, because TLS inspection and IDPS are core features that every SKU includes by default
Azure Firewall Basic, which includes TLS inspection and IDPS for small and medium-sized business environments
Azure Firewall Standard, which includes TLS inspection and IDPS alongside threat intelligence and web categories
Azure Firewall Premium, which adds outbound TLS inspection and fully managed IDPS to the Standard capabilities

stem: A small business deployed Azure Firewall Basic and enabled threat intelligence-based filtering. A report shows that traffic to a known malicious IP address was recorded as an alert but was still allowed through the firewall. What explains this?

choices.text: Threat intelligence in the Basic SKU runs in alert mode only; denying the traffic requires the Standard or Premium SKU
Threat intelligence filtering applies only to inbound traffic, so outbound connections to malicious IPs are always allowed
Threat intelligence filtering only works after the firewall has learned the traffic profile for several weeks of normal use
Threat intelligence filtering must be paired with a DDoS protection plan before it can block any connection on the firewall

stem: A large enterprise runs dozens of Azure Firewall instances across many subscriptions and in Virtual WAN secured hubs. The security team wants to define a common set of network and application rules once and apply it to all of these firewalls. What should it use?

choices.text: An Azure DDoS protection plan linked to every virtual network that hosts a firewall
Azure Key Vault storing the rule set as a secret that each firewall downloads at startup
Azure Firewall Manager with firewall policies applied to the firewalls in the tenant
A single network security group associated with the subnet of each firewall instance

stem: An architect is deciding whether to add Azure Firewall or rely only on network security groups. Which TWO capabilities does Azure Firewall provide that network security groups do not? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Allowing or denying traffic based on the source IP address, destination IP address, port and protocol of each flow
Association directly with a virtual machine's network interface so that its rules apply to that one virtual machine
Default rules that let resources in the same virtual network talk to each other while denying inbound internet traffic
Filtering of outbound traffic by fully qualified domain name in application rules, such as allowing one update site
Alerting on and denying traffic to known malicious IP addresses and domains using a Microsoft threat intelligence feed

stem: A company's public web application has been hit by SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts. The developers cannot patch every vulnerable page quickly, so the security team wants a central control that blocks these common web exploits before requests reach the app. What should it deploy?

choices.text: A network security group that allows only TCP port 443 inbound to the subnet that hosts the web servers
Azure Web Application Firewall with Application Gateway, using the managed rule set for common exploits
Azure Bastion in the application's virtual network, which hides the web servers from the internet entirely
Azure DDoS IP Protection on the application's public IP address, which blocks malicious HTTP payloads

stem: A team is about to enable Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway for a busy production site. It worries that the managed rules might block some legitimate requests. Microsoft's guidance suggests a way to start. What should the team do first?

choices.text: Run the WAF in detection mode for a short period, review the WAF logs, then add exceptions and switch to prevention
Run the WAF in prevention mode from day one, because detection mode turns off the managed rule sets entirely
Leave the WAF disabled and rely on a network security group until the developers finish their code review
Delete all managed rules and write only custom rules, because managed rules cannot be tuned with exclusions

stem: A streaming service has users on several continents and its web front end is delivered through Azure Front Door. It wants web exploits blocked close to where attackers are, at Microsoft's network edge, before requests ever enter its virtual networks. Where should it run Azure Web Application Firewall?

choices.text: On every virtual machine's network interface, by attaching the WAF policy to each VM's network security group
On Azure Firewall Premium, whose IDPS is the WAF engine that runs at the global network edge locations
On Azure Front Door, where the WAF policy is replicated to Microsoft's edge locations around the world
On Azure Application Gateway in each region, because WAF policies there inspect traffic at the global network edge

stem: A regional bank's customer portal sits behind Azure Application Gateway with Web Application Firewall enabled. Because the bank serves customers in only one country, it wants to block requests coming from all other countries or regions. What WAF feature meets this need?

choices.text: Detection mode, which logs requests from foreign countries so administrators can block them manually later
The OWASP Core Rule Set, which includes a default rule that blocks traffic from outside the home country
A custom rule that uses geo-filtering to allow the home country and block other countries or regions
The Bot Manager rule set, which classifies requests from foreign countries as bad bots and blocks them

stem: A company wants multilayered protection for a public web application in an Azure virtual network: resilience against volumetric network floods and protection against layer 7 attacks on the web requests themselves. Which TWO services together meet this goal? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Azure DDoS Protection on the virtual network, which mitigates layer 3 and layer 4 attacks
Application security groups, which hide the web servers' IP addresses from attackers on the internet
Azure Bastion in the virtual network, which removes the need for public IPs on the web servers
Azure Key Vault, which keeps the TLS certificate safe so attackers cannot flood the web endpoint
Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway, which inspects requests at layer 7

stem: An administrator created one Azure virtual network with a web subnet and a database subnet, assuming subnets keep traffic apart. A test shows that a web VM can reach every port on a database VM. No network security groups are associated with either subnet. Why can the VMs communicate?

choices.text: Azure only isolates subnets that have a route table attached, so the administrator must add a custom route to each subnet
Azure routes between subnets of a virtual network automatically, and no access controls exist between subnets by default
The database VM has a private IP address, and private IP addresses are always reachable from every Azure virtual network
Subnets in different availability zones always share traffic, so the VMs must be moved into a single zone to be isolated

stem: A company keeps its development and production workloads in two separate Azure virtual networks. A developer asks how the two environments can talk to each other if a later project ever needs it. What should the security team tell the developer?

choices.text: The networks can only reach each other through the internet using public IP addresses, because Azure has no private connection option
Resources in the two networks can already reach each other, because all virtual networks in a subscription are joined automatically
The networks can only be connected by moving both into one subscription and merging their address spaces into a single network
The networks stay separate until they are connected, for example with virtual network peering, after which their resources can communicate

stem: A network engineer is designing segmentation between the web, application and database subnets of one Azure virtual network. Which TWO options does Azure offer to filter network traffic between these subnets? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A network virtual appliance, such as a firewall, that inspects traffic passing between subnets
Azure Key Vault access policies, which decide which subnets may send traffic to one another
Custom route tables alone, which drop any packet that does not match one of their listed routes
Azure DDoS Protection, which blocks traffic between subnets that its traffic profile marks as unusual
Network security groups with inbound and outbound rules associated with the subnets

stem: A network security group on a subnet has two inbound rules: priority 100 denies TCP port 3389 from any source, and priority 200 allows TCP port 3389 from the IT department's IP range. IT staff report that they cannot connect over RDP. Why?

choices.text: Two rules for the same port cancel each other out, so the network security group falls back to its default allow rule
The deny rule has priority 100, which is processed before the allow rule at 200, and processing stops at the first match
The allow rule has priority 200, but rules with higher numbers apply only to outbound traffic and are ignored inbound
Allow rules are always evaluated before deny rules in a network security group, so the default rules must be blocking it

stem: An administrator creates a new network security group with no custom rules and associates it with a subnet that hosts a web server. Users on the internet cannot open the website on TCP port 80, but other VMs in the same virtual network can reach it. What explains this behaviour?

choices.text: The default AllowInternetOutBound rule blocks replies to internet users until an explicit outbound rule is created for port 80
The default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule blocks internet traffic unless the server sits behind an Azure load balancer
The default rules allow traffic within the virtual network but deny other inbound traffic, so an allow rule for port 80 is needed
The network security group blocks all traffic for one hour after creation while Azure learns the subnet's normal traffic patterns

stem: A virtual machine sits in a subnet that has network security group NSG-A, and its network interface has NSG-B. NSG-A allows inbound TCP 443 from the internet, but NSG-B has no rule for port 443 beyond its default rules. Will inbound HTTPS from the internet reach the VM?

choices.text: Yes, because a network security group on the subnet overrides any network security group on the network interface
No, because Azure does not allow network security groups on both a subnet and a network interface at once
Yes, because when two network security groups apply, Azure combines them and uses the most permissive rule
No, because NSG-A is processed first and then NSG-B, whose default DenyAllInbound rule blocks the traffic

stem: An application has web, logic and database VMs whose IP addresses change often as the team scales them. The security team wants network security group rules such as "only web servers may reach logic servers" without editing IP addresses in the rules every time. What should it use?

choices.text: Application security groups, which group the VMs' network interfaces by role so rules can use the group names
Azure Firewall Manager, which converts network security group rules into firewall policies keyed on VM names
Separate virtual networks for each tier, which remove the need for any network security group rules at all
Service tags, which Microsoft maintains to represent the IP address prefixes of the team's own web and logic VMs

stem: Administrators need RDP and SSH access to Azure virtual machines. The security team wants the VMs to have no public IP addresses and no internet-exposed management ports, and does not want to deploy and patch a jump-box VM. Which service should they use?

choices.text: A network security group rule that allows TCP 3389 and 22 from any source to each virtual machine's NIC
Azure Firewall with a DNAT rule that forwards a public port on the firewall to each VM's RDP or SSH port
Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway, publishing the RDP and SSH ports as web listeners
Azure Bastion deployed in the virtual network, connecting to VMs over TLS through the Azure portal or a native client

stem: A financial services firm uses Azure Bastion for administrator access to VMs. Its regulators now require that every remote session be recorded for later review. Which Azure Bastion SKU provides session recording?

choices.text: Standard, which adds session recording together with native client and shareable links
Basic, which records sessions as part of its dedicated deployment with fixed capacity
Premium, which includes all Standard features and adds session recording for compliance
Developer, which records each session on the shared infrastructure for one VM at a time

stem: A help desk manager is preparing a short briefing on Azure Bastion for new administrators. Which TWO statements about Azure Bastion are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Administrators must first connect to the virtual network with a point-to-site VPN client before Bastion will accept them
Target virtual machines do not need a public IP address, because Bastion reaches them by their private IP addresses
Bastion inspects HTTP requests to the virtual machines and blocks SQL injection before it reaches the web servers
Each target virtual machine must run a Bastion agent that opens an outbound tunnel to the Azure portal for sessions
Bastion connections to virtual machines use RDP or SSH carried over TLS on port 443 from the portal or a native client

stem: A development team stores a database connection string and an API key in the application's configuration file in source control. The security team wants these values stored centrally with tightly controlled access, logged when they are read, and kept out of the code. What should the team use?

choices.text: Azure Bastion, which stores administrator credentials and passes them to the app when it connects
Azure Key Vault secrets, which the app retrieves at runtime after authenticating with a managed identity
Azure Web Application Firewall, which hides the connection string from HTTP requests that reach the app
A network security group rule that blocks access to the configuration file from outside the virtual network

stem: A company must store its encryption keys so that they are protected by hardware security modules and never leave the HSM boundary, to meet an internal standard requiring FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware. Which Azure Key Vault option meets this requirement?

choices.text: Either tier, because all key vaults are encrypted at rest and therefore every stored key counts as HSM-protected
The Standard tier, which stores every key inside a dedicated HSM that is assigned to each individual vault
The Premium tier, which offers HSM-protected keys generated and protected by FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs
The Standard tier with soft delete turned on, which moves the keys into an HSM once they are marked as deleted

stem: Auditors worry that a rogue administrator could delete a key vault and immediately purge it, permanently destroying the encryption keys that protect company data. Soft delete is already on. Which Key Vault setting ensures deleted vaults and keys cannot be permanently removed until the retention period ends?

choices.text: Purge protection, which blocks purging of deleted vaults and objects until the retention period has passed
Key Vault logging to Azure Monitor, which reverses deletions by replaying the logged operations afterwards
Key autorotation, which creates a new key version on a schedule so deleted keys are restored automatically
The Premium tier, which stores keys in HSMs that refuse any delete request from an administrator account
